_comment: One description of this standalone lesson build. Every tool in ../lesson-app-tools/ reads this instead of hardcoding a directory and a lesson list. Order here IS the teaching order and IS the unit number: unit N is lessons[N-1]. build-hub.py asserts its card order against this array. Eight lessons, one per Cambridge 0096 Stage 4 sub-strand, with Statistics and Probability together as Grade 2 does.
subject: mathematics

lessons.title: Big Numbers and Below Zero
lessons.materials: A long strip of paper or string marked as a number line running well past zero in both directions, and a printed thermometer if you have one. Walking along a real line past zero is what makes a negative number a place rather than just a minus sign.
lessons.atHome: Look at a weather forecast or a freezer thermometer for temperatures below zero, and put them in order from coldest to warmest. Find a big number in a newspaper and say what each digit is worth.

warmUp.q: Let's warm up. In Grade 3 you worked with hundreds. What is the 4 worth in 435?
warmUp.why: The 4 is in the hundreds column, so it is worth 400. Today you will go on into the thousands, and below zero.

lessons.title: Patterns and Square Numbers
lessons.materials: About 25 counters or buttons to lay out in square arrays - 2 by 2, 3 by 3, 4 by 4 - and to split into pairs for odd and even. Building a square number as an actual square of counters is what makes the name make sense.
lessons.atHome: Make square numbers with coins or buttons: 2 by 2, 3 by 3, 4 by 4, and count each square. Then add two odd numbers a few times and see what kind of number you always get.

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you worked with big numbers and numbers below zero. Warm up: is 7 odd or even?
warmUp.why: 7 counters make 3 pairs and 1 left over, so 7 is odd. Today you will see what odd and even numbers do, and find square numbers.

lessons.title: Ways to Calculate
lessons.materials: Counters or a hundred square for checking working, and something with a total to estimate first, such as a shopping list. Estimating before calculating, and checking the exact answer against the estimate, is a habit worth doing with real numbers.
lessons.atHome: Before adding up a shopping list, estimate the total, then work it out exactly and compare. Pick a number such as 24 and find every pair of numbers that multiply to make it.

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you found patterns and square numbers. Warm up: what is 6 times 4?
warmUp.why: 6 fours are 24. Today you will estimate, add, take away, multiply and divide.

lessons.title: Parts of a Whole
lessons.materials: A paper circle or strip to fold or cut into eighths, and about 20 beans or buttons to share into equal groups. Folding a strip into eighths is what makes three eighths a real, comparable amount next to a half, not just two fractions on a page.
lessons.atHome: Cut a paper circle into eighths and compare: which is bigger, three eighths or one half? Find a quarter of 20 beans by sharing them into four equal groups.

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you calculated with big numbers. Warm up: what is half of 10?
warmUp.why: 10 shared into 2 equal parts gives 5 in each. Today you will work with fractions and percentages.

lessons.title: Telling the Time
lessons.materials: A clock with hands, and a real bus timetable or TV guide printed in 24-hour time. Converting a real 24-hour time into the 12-hour time you say out loud is the whole of this lesson.
lessons.atHome: Read a bus timetable or a TV guide written in 24-hour time, change a few of the times into 12-hour time, and work out how long a journey or a programme lasts.

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you worked with fractions. Warm up: how many minutes are there in half an hour?
warmUp.why: An hour is 60 minutes, and half of 60 is 30. Today you will read clocks, timetables and calendars.

lessons.title: Shape and Measures
lessons.materials: Square sticky notes or squared paper to cover a surface and count for area, and a corner - a book or a set square - to check angles against. Covering a real table mat with squares is what makes area a count of squares rather than a formula.
lessons.atHome: Cover a table mat with square sticky notes to find its area. Look around the room for right angles, and for acute angles (smaller than a right angle) and obtuse ones (bigger).

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you worked with time. Warm up: how many faces does a cube have?
warmUp.why: A cube has 6 square faces, just like a dice. Today you will look at solids, symmetry, angles and area.

lessons.title: Where Things Are
lessons.materials: Squared paper for a coordinate grid, and room to stand and point using all eight compass directions. Walking along one direction and then up to reach a point is what makes a coordinate a route rather than two numbers in brackets.
lessons.atHome: Draw a grid with numbered lines on paper and hide 'treasure' at a point such as (3, 2) for your child to find, going along first and then up. Then take turns giving directions using the eight compass points.

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you looked at shapes and measures. Warm up: the sun rises in the east. Which direction is opposite east?
warmUp.why: East and west are opposite each other. Today you will use compass points and coordinates.

lessons.title: Asking, Sorting and Chance
lessons.materials: Paper for a Venn or Carroll diagram, and a coin or spinner for a chance experiment. Sorting real answers into two overlapping circles is what makes a Venn diagram mean something, rather than a shape already filled in.
lessons.atHome: Ask everyone at home a question, sort the answers in a Carroll or Venn diagram, and talk about events that are certain, likely, maybe or impossible, such as rain tomorrow.

warmUp.q: Last lesson, you used compass points and coordinates. Warm up: you toss a coin. How many ways can it land?
warmUp.why: A coin can land heads or tails, so there are 2 ways. Today you will collect data, draw charts and talk about chance.

_explorationStepsComment: Teaching steps with no right answer, so check-judging.py does not count them as failures: manipulatives a child explores rather than answers. An entry that stops firing fails the gate - it means the step now judges, or is gone.
